Hearing parents of deaf children, look lively.

SO MUCH oralist rhetoric boils down to "If you teach your child ASL, you'll lose them to the terrible Deafs." 

As an imperfect father (and mediocre signer) I would like to stake my position clearly: we want our kids to go no-contact because of our personality disorders, not lack of language.

Language deprivation is going to make for tough family relationships to start with—even if (especially if) it sabotages your kid's independence. And if it doesn't, dinner table syndrome very well might—there's no better reason to go low-or-no contact with fam if you don't get anything FROM contact.

But there are even higher-level meta-resentments that I see with the deaf children of oralist parents:
Feeling like you weren't worth learning sign for. 
Feeling like you were kept from community for selfish reasons. 
Feeling constant pressure to "be normal."

Learning ASL isn't a panacea for parents; you've still got to actually, y'know, raise your child. This isn't simple, but staying away from that foundational mistake means that at least you'll know why you weren't invited to your Deaf kid's 7-apex Wiccan furry polycule handfasting in 2045.

I joke, but both the no-contact trend in the wider world and its older cousin in deaf/hearing families comes from forms of abuse that have been recognized by professionals for decades, but which have been either invisible or trivialized until very recently in American culture.

As is often the case, it takes multiple generations to move from recognizing a problem, to paying it lip-service, to acting in real ways to solve these problems. I feel like the "hearing parents don't learn sign" thing is now on that third step...

On October 19, 1943, researchers at Rutgers University isolated an antibiotic that would change the treatment of tuberculosis. Its name was streptomycin, and its discovery offered hope against a disease that had killed millions and for which no reliably effective antibiotic treatment existed: 🧵
The discovery came from a research team led by microbiologist Selman Waksman, who had spent years studying microorganisms found in soil.

Waksman believed that soil bacteria could produce substances capable of killing other harmful microbes. His laboratory developed systematic methods for testing these organisms in the search for new antibiotics.
The breakthrough came through Albert Schatz, a graduate student working in Waksman's laboratory. On October 19, 1943, Schatz isolated streptomycin from Streptomyces griseus, a soil microorganism.

The substance proved effective against bacteria responsible for several serious diseases, including the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. This was significant because penicillin, the antibiotic transforming the treatment of many infections at the time, was ineffective against tuberculosis.

Elizabeth Bugie contributed to the testing and study of streptomycin. Schatz, Bugie and Waksman published their findings in 1944. Their work laid the foundation for further experiments to determine whether the drug could safely treat tuberculosis in animals and humans.

Researchers still had to establish its effectiveness, determine appropriate doses and produce enough of the drug for medical use. Clinical research conducted with the Mayo Clinic helped demonstrate its value.
In 1946, a major British study began testing streptomycin for pulmonary tuberculosis and became an important milestone in the development of modern clinical trials.

In 1952, Waksman received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discovery of streptomycin. Schatz, whose direct laboratory work was central to isolating the antibiotic, was not included in the award.
The dispute over credit continued for years, and Rutgers later acknowledged Schatz's status as a co discoverer. Bugie's contribution is also recognized in the university's historical account.

Streptomycin was not a universal cure, and bacteria could develop resistance to it. Nevertheless, it provided the first effective antibiotic treatment for tuberculosis and transformed the outlook for many patients who previously had few effective treatment options.

The discovery at Rutgers on October 19, 1943, showed the potential of soil microorganisms to produce life saving medicines and helped open a new chapter in the fight against infectious disease.
